claims.text: A machine-learning model trained on experimental and defect-inclusive computational data will predict the thermal conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional analytical models.
The proposed model will apply across the nearly 0–200 K regime.
The proposed model will apply across the 300–1200 K regime.
The proposed model will apply to bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The improvement in prediction accuracy arises because the model can learn the effects of defects and disorder.
Traditional analytical models omit defect and disorder effects because they assume perfect crystals.
Machine-learning models can capture complex, non-analytical relationships among defects, disorder, and thermal conductivity.
Atomic-scale defects and oxygen impurities are relevant structural features governing the proposed conductivity prediction.
The model will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to analytical models in both temperature regimes and for the oxygen-containing specimen.
Analytical predictions for defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystals typically underestimate defect and impurity effects.
The proposed model is applicable only to bulk samples having defect and impurity concentrations similar to those represented in its training data.
Extrapolation to extreme defect concentrations or nanostructured forms may reduce prediction accuracy.
The degree of improvement depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
Insufficient defect-inclusive training data could limit model accuracy.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to analytical models in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
